sections.h2: Which bill applies to your address
sections.html:
Lafayette Parish packs six municipalities into 269 square miles of Acadiana, almost none of it water. The city of Lafayette is both seat and largest town. Broussard (partly in St. Martin Parish), Carencro, Scott, Youngsville and Duson (partly in Acadia Parish) have their own governments, while Milton and Ossun are unincorporated communities.

Where the house stands decides what you pay and to whom. A house in Youngsville, Scott or Carencro is taxed differently from one inside the City of Lafayette or on unincorporated land, so find out whether a town levies tax on you before you open the bill.

ContactDetails

About 100,000 notices leave the Sheriff's Office each November. Pay by December 31 to avoid a penalty.

The Sheriff also collects for several towns. Carencro and Youngsville joined the arrangement in 2004, and Scott and Duson followed in 2008. Residents of those places get one combined bill covering town and parish tax, and the Sheriff divides the money afterward. One check does the job.

  • Ways to pay: online at the Sheriff's Web Tax Site, or in person with cash, personal check or credit card.
  • Counter hours run 7:30 a.m. to 4:45 p.m. Monday to Thursday and 8:00 a.m. to 4:15 p.m. on Friday.
  • Online e-check and card payments cost a transaction fee.

Inside the City of Lafayette the picture changes: the city sends its own tax bill, so you may owe two payments.

The Assessor's role is to identify and value property. It does not decide the size of your bill, since rates come from the city-parish government, school board, sheriff and other taxing bodies.

Values are redone at least once every four years under state law, and can change annually if the market moves. Appraisers lead with comparable sales, then test the result with cost and income methods. The website offers a tax estimator, a property search and a parcel map. Check what the county shows for your house before you talk price with a buyer. An assessment is not an offer, but a wide gap deserves a call.

Most owners use the homestead exemption. A home you live in, with up to 160 acres, gets $7,500 of assessed value (equal to $75,000 of market value) taken off state, parish and special taxes. The owner's pool, pool house or storage shed counts too, but a second dwelling or a commercial building on the land does not.

A separate freeze holds the assessed value at its January 1, 2025 level until the home is sold or remodeled, and it stops at the end of December before a sale. You need a homestead exemption and one of the following:

  • Age 65 or older.
  • A permanent, total disability determined by a court, state or federal agency.
  • A service-connected disability rating of 50% or more.

Adjusted gross income may not exceed $100,000. A freeze does not stop millage changes, so the bill can still rise. Farmland is valued by its use if it covers three acres or more, or if it earned at least $2,000 gross in each of the last four years.

Talk first to a deputy assessor, and arrive with proof. A reduction requires showing the assessment exceeds market value and why. Accept the deputy's answer and the matter ends there.

Still unhappy? The Lafayette Consolidated Council hears appeals in September on dates it sets in August, and it rules after reviewing your material and the Assessor's. The next level is the Louisiana Tax Commission. Its decisions stand unless you take them to district court within thirty days.

Call the Assessor each summer for the current hearing board and filing date.

Past December 31, unpaid tax earns interest, and the house may be offered at the online tax sale on the first Wednesday in June. After a tax sale, the Louisiana Constitution gives the owner three years from recordation to redeem, paying the price, costs, a 5% penalty and 1% monthly interest.

If no one bids, the property is adjudicated. Applicants cannot use Lafayette Consolidated Government's disposition process until it has been adjudicated for three years running. Public bidding opens at no less than 75% of the Assessor's fair market value, and a second round about a month later opens at 33%. Outstanding taxes and liens are waived when the right affidavit is recorded, and applicants are urged to hire an attorney with title experience.

Until the act of sale to the applicant is recorded, the owner can still redeem by paying every tax, lien and fee owed to the city and the Sheriff. It costs far less to clear arrears early.

A few chores are worth doing ahead of time. Look up your assessment with the Assessor's property search. Find out whether you hold the homestead exemption or the freeze, since neither carries over to the buyer. Confirm which bill covers your address, and pay each one before December 31 if you can, because the interest clock starts on January 1.

If you are behind, call the Sheriff's tax office at 337-236-5400 for the amount due. If the house sits in the City of Lafayette, ask the city for its figure too. Having both numbers in hand lets you compare a cash offer with a listing sale on the same footing.

Bring the most recent notice to any conversation with a buyer or title agent. It shows the parcel, the assessed value and the amounts billed, which answers most of their first questions before they have to ask.

What you owe is paid out of the sale proceeds. Your closing agent can order a tax certificate under R.S. 9:2901, a document that lists unpaid state, parish, municipal and levee district taxes, leaving out the year of the sale.

A cash buyer needs no mortgage approval or appraisal, so sales burdened by tax bills, an inheritance, tenants or repairs can close sooner. The new owner then files a homestead claim and the Assessor records the change.

  1. Request payoff figures from the Sheriff, and from the city if the house lies inside Lafayette.
  2. The closing agent orders the tax certificate.
  3. At signing, the balance is deducted from what you receive.
  4. Confirm the act reaches the Lafayette Parish Clerk of Court for recording. Our clerk guide has the fees and steps.

faqs.q: Who collects property tax in Lafayette Parish?
faqs.a: The Sheriff's Office tax department mails about 100,000 notices each November and collects payments. The City of Lafayette bills its own city tax separately.

faqs.q: What is the Lafayette Parish tax deadline?
faqs.a: The deadline to pay without penalty is December 31 each year. Unpaid amounts accrue interest and can lead to the tax sale in June.

faqs.q: What is the Lafayette Parish homestead exemption?
faqs.a: It exempts $7,500 of assessed value, equal to $75,000 of market value, for an owner-occupied home on up to 160 acres. You claim it with the Assessor.

faqs.q: Can seniors freeze their Lafayette Parish assessment?
faqs.a: Owners 65 or older, or with a qualifying disability, can apply for a freeze if they hold a homestead exemption and have adjusted gross income of $100,000 or less. It fixes the January 1, 2025 value.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Lafayette Parish house with back taxes?
faqs.a: Yes. The taxes are paid from the sale proceeds at closing. Selling before adjudication keeps you in control and stops interest from growing.
